query: In Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs phase stability and why, with relevance to retaining desirable combinations of high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness? Specify a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries of the hypothesis, supporting prior evidence, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The deliberate formation and controlled volume fraction of an ordered γ′ precipitate phase in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs stabilizes the FCC matrix, resulting in enhanced high-temperature strength, improved radiation tolerance, and superior cryogenic toughness.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-cast HEA that is predominantly a single-phase FCC structure with minimal γ′ precipitate formation.
generation.intervention: Systematically adjust the alloy composition by increasing Al (and optionally Ti) content to promote nucleation of a dispersed, nano-scale γ′ precipitate phase while keeping the composition within a range that avoids brittle intermetallic formation.
generation.conditions: Mechanical testing under high-temperature exposure, irradiation experiments, and cryogenic deformation tests.
generation.structural_mediator: The presence of a finely dispersed, nano-scale ordered γ′ phase within the FCC matrix that impedes dislocation motion and stabilizes the microstructure.
generation.mechanism: The controlled precipitation of the γ′ phase provides precipitation strengthening by hindering dislocation motion in the FCC matrix. This not only increases high-temperature strength but also creates a heterogeneity that enables deformation twinning at low temperatures and acts as defect sinks during irradiation, thereby enhancing overall stability and performance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Alloys with a well-controlled γ′ precipitate volume fraction will exhibit higher yield and tensile strengths at elevated temperatures, reduced radiation-induced defect accumulation, and improved cryogenic toughness compared to a baseline alloy lacking significant γ′ formation.
generation.baseline: An equiatomic Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEA with negligible γ′ precipitate formation.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects are confined to compositions that yield a uniform, nano-scale γ′ phase; exceeding the optimal Al (and Ti) content may lead to unwanted brittle intermetallic phases that compromise ductility.
generation.uncertainty: The precise compositional window that yields the optimal γ/γ′ balance and the quantitative impact of the γ′ phase on long-term radiation tolerance remain to be firmly established.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs: one tuned to promote the formation of a dispersed γ′ phase and a baseline sample with minimal γ′ formation. Subject both sets to high-temperature mechanical tests, ion irradiation, and cryogenic deformation analysis.

High-temperature yield and tensile strength measurements
Radiation-induced defect density (via ion irradiation experiments)

falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the composition designed to promote γ′ formation does not exhibit a significantly higher volume fraction of γ′ or fails to demonstrate statistically improved mechanical properties and radiation tolerance compared to the baseline sample, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In particular, the extraordinary ductility and fracture toughness of FCC-structured HEAs at ambient temperature and cryogenic temperatures have garnered significant attention [,,,,]. The low yield strength of FCC-structured HEAs, which is typically just 200 MPa in the as-cast form, is a significant disadvantage, as it is significantly less than the necessary strength of metallic structural materials [,]. To overcome these limitations in mechanical properties, a proposed method is to manufacture an HEA composed of a multicomponent FCC-HEA matrix with an ordered FCC structure (L12) precipitated phase, i.e., the γ′ phase, by adding Al + Ti. An HEA based on a γ + γ′ alloy system exhibited excellent thermal stability, coarsening resistance, and strength retention around a temperature of 800 °C [,,,]. The γ′ phase is an ordered phase with an almost exact stoichiometric composition ((Ni, Co)3(Ti, Al)) in the Ni-Co-Fe-Cr-Al-Ti HEA, with γ′ depending on the Al + Ti content []. Numerous studies have been conducted on the γ′ phase’s formation and mechanical properties [,]. A high content of Al + Ti leads to the formation of precipitate phases such as Ni2AlTi. Based on the predictive model and SHAP interpretation, a strategic approach to optimizing Al–Ti–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs for high hardness includes: (i) increasing Al and Ti contents, which are dominant in enhancing hardness via lattice distortion and precipitation strengthening; (ii) maintaining a Ti/Al ratio between 1.2 and 2.0 to favor duplex phase formation (FCC + L12 or FCC + BCC); (iii) retaining Cr and Co at moderate levels (10–20 at. 1%) to assist in solid solution and phase strengthening; and (iv) minimizing Ni and Fe content when hardness is prioritized over ductility, as both tend to stabilize FCC phases that reduce hardness. These guidelines, derived from both data-driven insights and physical interpretation, provide a practical reference for composition design under laser additive manufacturing constraints.

High-entropy alloys (HEAs), which contain at least four principal elements in (near-)equiatomic ratios, have attracted extensive attention because of their interesting properties. In the early stage of the development of HEAs, researchers wanted to seek single-phase solid-solution alloys because they considered that intermetallics are brittle and may degenerate the properties of HEAs. However, the fact that in most engineering alloys, secondary phases contribute significantly to the alloy properties is also true in HEAs; many reported HEAs that can overcome the strength–ductility trade-off contain two or more phases. Proper control of the type, shape, size, volume fraction, and distribution of precipitation phases is critical for the development of the HEAs with high strength while retaining sufficient ductility,. Ni3Al-type ordered L12 phases, which are ductile and coherent with FCC matrices, are one important class of strengthening phases in FCC-based alloys such as superalloys, and the strengthening effects depend prominently on the volume fractions of these precipitates.
